title: The Eastern Question
subtitle: 1774–1900 · Russia, Britain and France on the Straits, the Nile and the Gulf: Capitulations, Protectorates, the Suez Canal, the Debt and the Great Game

categories.label: Power
categories.subtitle: Catherine and Nicholas, Napoleon and Palmerston, Disraeli and Gladstone, Bismarck and the sultans

entries.label: Catherine II and the Greek project
entries.hint: Catherine II, who after Küçük Kaynarca (1774) annexed Crimea in 1783 and with Potemkin built the new Black Sea fleet and the port of Sevastopol, conceived with Joseph II the so-called Greek Project of partitioning the Ottoman lands and restoring a Byzantine empire under her grandson Constantine; Russia thus became the principal power on the Black Sea and a claimant to the Straits and to the protection of the Orthodox.
entries.note: Isabel de Madariaga, Russia in the Age of Catherine the Great (1981); Matthew Anderson, The Eastern Question 1774–1923 (1966); Treaty of Küçük Kaynarca (1774).

entries.label: Nicholas I and the sick man
entries.hint: Nicholas I, who supported Greek independence in 1828–1829 and signed the Treaty of Hünkâr İskelesi in 1833, spoke in January 1853 to the British ambassador Seymour of a sick man, a very sick man, at the point of death, and proposed to divide his inheritance; the British refused and the Holy Places dispute became the pretext for the Crimean War, in which Nicholas died in 1855.
entries.note: Anderson 1966; Seymour's dispatch (Jan.–Feb. 1853); Orlando Figes, Crimea (2010).

entries.label: Napoleon and the Oriental policy of France
entries.hint: Bonaparte, who sought to strike at Britain's route to India, led the expedition of 1798 into Egypt with 38,000 troops and 167 scholars, issued proclamations to the Egyptians and the Ottoman sultan and, at Tilsit in 1807, negotiated with Alexander I a division of the Ottoman provinces; the Description de l'Égypte (1809–1829), its great scholarly report, was the foundation of Egyptology.
entries.note: Juan Cole, Napoleon's Egypt (2007); Description de l'Égypte (1809–1829); Anderson 1966.

entries.label: Palmerston, Stratford Canning and British policy
entries.hint: Viscount Palmerston, foreign secretary and prime minister, held that Britain's interests in the route to India and the Mediterranean demanded the preservation of the Ottoman Empire as a buffer against Russia and Muhammad Ali, and with the ambassador Stratford Canning at Istanbul (1842–1858) promoted reforms, the Tanzimat, trade treaties and the Crimean War as a means to that end.
entries.note: Anderson 1966; Harold Temperley, England and the Near East: The Crimea (1936); Kenneth Bourne, Palmerston (1982).

entries.label: Disraeli and Gladstone
entries.hint: Benjamin Disraeli, who bought the Khedive's Suez Canal shares for four million pounds in 1875, sent the fleet to the Straits in 1878 and brought back from Berlin peace with honour and Cyprus; William Gladstone, in the pamphlet Bulgarian Horrors (1876) and the Midlothian campaign, rejected support for the Turks on moral grounds and as prime minister ordered the occupation of Egypt in 1882.
entries.note: Richard Shannon, Gladstone (1999); Robert Blake, Disraeli (1966); Gladstone, Bulgarian Horrors and the Question of the East (1876).

entries.label: Bismarck, Wilhelm II and Germany in the East
entries.hint: Bismarck, presiding at the Congress of Berlin as an honest broker, said the Eastern Question was not worth the bones of a Pomeranian grenadier; after 1888 Wilhelm II sent military missions to Istanbul, took up the Anatolian and Baghdad railways and visited the sultan in 1889 and 1898, and Germany became the Ottoman state's closest great-power patron.
entries.note: Bismarck's Reichstag speech (5 Dec. 1876); Jonathan McMurray, Distant Ties (2001); Anderson 1966.

entries.label: Muhammad Ali and the Egyptian question
entries.hint: Muhammad Ali's armies took Syria in 1831–1833 and again in 1839, and his fleet defeated the sultan's; his challenge forced the powers to intervene: Russia in 1833 by the Hünkâr İskelesi treaty, and Britain, Austria, Prussia and Russia in 1840 in the London Convention, so that the Egyptian question became the first European crisis in which the great powers agreed to maintain the empire against its own vassal.
entries.note: Khaled Fahmy, All the Pasha's Men (1997); Anderson 1966; Convention of London (15 July 1840).

categories.label: Conflict
categories.subtitle: The Russian wars, Napoleon's expedition, the Greek and Egyptian crises, the Crimean War, 1877–1878, the occupation of Egypt and the Great Game

entries.label: The Russo-Ottoman wars
entries.loc: The Danube and the Black Sea
entries.hint: Between 1768 and 1829 Russia and the Ottomans fought four wars (1768–1774, 1787–1792, 1806–1812 and 1828–1829), in which Russian armies took Crimea, the northern Black Sea coast, Bessarabia (1812) and the Danube mouths; each ended with a treaty at Küçük Kaynarca, Jassy, Bucharest and Adrianople that extended Russia's claims to protect the Orthodox and to free passage of the Straits.
entries.note: Treaties of Küçük Kaynarca (1774), Jassy (1792), Bucharest (1812), Adrianople (1829); Virginia Aksan, Ottoman Wars 1700–1870 (2007).

entries.label: Napoleon's invasion of Egypt and Syria
entries.hint: The French landing at Alexandria in July 1798, the victory of the Pyramids and Nelson's destruction of the French fleet at Aboukir Bay in August cut the army off; Bonaparte's march to Syria was stopped at Acre in 1799 and the British and Ottoman forces defeated the French in 1801, a first European invasion of a main Ottoman province that made Egypt the key of the route to India.
entries.note: Al-Jabarti, Aja'ib al-athar; Cole 2007; Anderson 1966.

entries.label: The Greek war and Navarino
entries.hint: The Greek revolt that began in 1821 won the sympathy of the educated public in Europe, among them Lord Byron, who died at Missolonghi in 1824, and the intervention of the three powers, with their fleet's destruction of the Ottoman–Egyptian fleet at Navarino in October 1827, led with Russia's war of 1828–1829 to the independence of a Greek kingdom in 1830–1832, the first state to be carved from the Ottoman empire by the powers.
entries.note: David Brewer, The Flame of Freedom (2001); Anderson 1966; Treaty of London (1827).

entries.group: The Scramble and the Great Game
entries.label: The French conquest of Algeria and Tunisia
entries.hint: The French army landed near Algiers in June 1830 and took the city in July, ended the regency's rule from Istanbul and in a war of seventeen years against Abd al-Qadir and the following campaigns conquered the country; the occupation of Tunisia in 1881 with the Treaty of Bardo and Italy's interest in Tripoli were stages in the loss of the Ottoman North African provinces.
entries.note: Treaty of Bardo (12 May 1881); Julia Clancy-Smith, Rebel and Saint (1994); Anderson 1966.

entries.group: The Scramble and the Great Game
entries.label: The Great Game in Persia and Afghanistan
entries.hint: The rivalry of Britain and Russia in Central Asia and Persia led to the first Afghan war of 1839–1842 with the loss of an army of 16,500 in the retreat from Kabul, the Persian siege of Herat in 1837–1838 and the Anglo-Persian war of 1856–1857, the Russian conquest of Khiva and Bukhara and the Penjdeh incident of 1885, which nearly led to a war; the phrase the Great Game was used by Arthur Conolly.
entries.note: Peter Hopkirk, The Great Game (1990); Malcolm Yapp, Strategies of British India (1980); Anderson 1966.

entries.label: The Syrian crisis of 1840
entries.hint: When Mahmud II died in 1839 and Muhammad Ali's army defeated the sultan's at Nizip, Britain, Austria, Russia and Prussia, without France, which backed the pasha, signed the Convention of London in July 1840 and, after the bombardment of Beirut and Acre in the autumn by an Anglo-Austrian-Ottoman fleet, forced Muhammad Ali to give up Syria for the hereditary rule of Egypt; the Straits Convention of 1841 closed the Straits to all warships in peacetime.
entries.note: Convention of London (1840); Straits Convention (13 July 1841); Anderson 1966; Fahmy 1997.

entries.label: The Crimean War
entries.hint: The dispute over the Holy Places and the Russian demand for a protectorate over the Orthodox of the Ottoman empire led to Nicholas's occupation of the Danubian principalities in 1853, the Ottoman declaration of war in October and the Russian destruction of a fleet at Sinope; Britain and France joined in 1854, and after the siege of Sevastopol, the first war reported by telegraph and photograph, the Treaty of Paris of 1856 neutralised the Black Sea.
entries.note: Figes 2010; Treaty of Paris (1856); Andrew Lambert, The Crimean War (1990).

entries.label: The Balkan crisis and the Congress of Berlin
entries.hint: The Herzegovinian revolt of 1875, the Bulgarian rising of 1876 and the Russo-Turkish war of 1877–1878 led to San Stefano and the Congress of Berlin, in which Britain, Austria and Germany reduced Russia's gains, so that Bulgaria was divided, Bosnia went to Austria and Cyprus to Britain, a settlement that left a series of Balkan grievances and the Ottomans a European lifeline.
entries.note: Treaties of San Stefano (3 March 1878) and Berlin (13 July 1878); Richard Millman, Britain and the Eastern Question 1875–1878 (1979).

entries.group: The Scramble and the Great Game
entries.label: The occupation of Egypt
entries.hint: After the debt crisis, the dual control of Britain and France, the military revolt of Colonel Ahmad Urabi and the riots in Alexandria in June 1882, the British fleet bombarded Alexandria on 11 July and an army under Wolseley crushed Urabi at Tel el-Kebir on 13 September; Britain promised to withdraw as soon as order was restored, and stayed until 1956.
entries.note: Juan Cole, Colonialism and Revolution in the Middle East (1993); Alexander Schölch, Egypt for the Egyptians! (1981); Lord Cromer, Modern Egypt (1908).

categories.label: Order
categories.subtitle: Küçük Kaynarca, the Straits conventions, the Paris and Berlin treaties, the Capitulations and the Mixed Courts

entries.label: The Straits regime
entries.hint: Under Küçük Kaynarca in 1774 Russian merchant ships were granted free passage of the Straits, the treaty of Hünkâr İskelesi of 1833 promised their closure to other warships, and the London Straits Convention of 1841, signed by the five powers and the Porte, established the rule that the Straits would be closed to foreign warships in peacetime, which was reaffirmed in 1856, amended in 1871 and remained the basis until Montreux in 1936.
entries.note: Treaties of Küçük Kaynarca (1774), Hünkâr İskelesi (1833), London (1841); Montreux Convention (1936); Anderson 1966.

entries.label: The Capitulations and the Mixed Courts
entries.hint: The French capitulations of 1740 and their renewals gave Europeans in the Ottoman lands exemption from local courts and taxes, the right to consular jurisdiction and, with the berat system, the protection of local Christians and Jews employed by foreign missions; in Egypt, in 1875, the Mixed Courts, with European and Egyptian judges, replaced the consular courts in civil cases but applied the French code to Europeans.
entries.note: Maurits van den Boogert, The Capitulations and the Ottoman Legal System (2005); Jasper Brinton, The Mixed Courts of Egypt (1930); Anderson 1966.

entries.label: The treaty of Balta Limanı and the free-trade regime
entries.hint: The Anglo-Ottoman commercial convention of 1838, which abolished the state monopolies and internal customs on British goods and fixed import duties at 3 per cent, was followed by similar treaties with France and others and, after 1861 revisions, made the Ottoman Empire one of the most open markets of the world, at the cost of the local crafts.
entries.note: Convention of Balta Limanı (16 August 1838); Şevket Pamuk, The Ottoman Empire and European Capitalism (1987); Roderic Davison, Reform in the Ottoman Empire (1963).

entries.label: The Treaty of Paris and the London Conference
entries.hint: The Treaty of Paris of 30 March 1856 neutralised the Black Sea, closed it to warships and arsenals, guaranteed the independence and integrity of the Ottoman Empire and put the Danubian principalities under the guarantee of the powers; Russia, taking advantage of France's defeat in 1870, had the neutralisation clauses removed at the London Conference of 1871.
entries.note: Treaty of Paris (1856); London Protocol (13 March 1871); Anderson 1966.

entries.label: The Treaty of Berlin
entries.hint: The treaty of the Congress of Berlin recognised the independence of Serbia, Montenegro and Romania, made Bulgaria an autonomous principality and left Eastern Rumelia with the Porte, placed Bosnia and Herzegovina under the Austrian occupation and gave Russia Kars, Ardahan and Batum; Article 61 required the Porte to carry out reforms in the Armenian provinces under the powers' supervision, a clause that was later used for the Armenian question.
entries.note: Treaty of Berlin (13 July 1878), articles 1, 25, 58, 61; Anderson 1966.

categories.label: Belief
categories.subtitle: The Holy Places, the protectorates over churches, the Damascus Affair and the missions

entries.label: The Russian pilgrims and the Orthodox protectorate
entries.hint: After Küçük Kaynarca Russia took the claim to protect Orthodox Christians in the Ottoman Empire, and tens of thousands of Russian pilgrims came to Jerusalem each year, often 10,000 in the later years of the nineteenth century, with a Russian compound built in 1860–1864 and the Russian Palestine Society after 1882 owning churches, hospices and schools.
entries.note: Theofanis Stavrou and Peter Weisensel (eds.), Russian Pilgrims in Jerusalem (1985); Derek Hopwood, The Russian Presence in Syria and Palestine (1969).

entries.label: The missions of the churches
entries.hint: The American Board of Commissioners for Foreign Missions began its work in Beirut in 1823 and set up the Syrian Protestant College in 1866, Robert College in 1863, and the French Jesuits the Université Saint-Joseph in Beirut in 1875; the missions, with the Russian Palestine Society (1882) and the German Templers, were agencies of the powers' influence and of education, with the printing press of the Syrian Nahda.
entries.note: Ussama Makdisi, Artillery of Heaven (2008); Frank Stone, Academies for Anatolia (1984); Anderson 1966.

entries.label: The Anglican bishopric and the protection of the Jews
entries.hint: Britain and Prussia founded a joint Protestant bishopric at Jerusalem in 1841, with Michael Solomon Alexander, a converted Jew, as the first bishop, and Palmerston made the protection of the Jews of Palestine a part of British policy in 1838 by appointing a vice-consul at Jerusalem, William Young; in the Damascus Affair of 1840 Moses Montefiore and Adolphe Crémieux went to the East to defend Jews accused of ritual murder.
entries.note: Barbara Tuchman, Bible and Sword (1956); Jonathan Frankel, The Damascus Affair (1997); Anderson 1966.

entries.label: The Holy Places dispute
entries.hint: The quarrel of Latin and Orthodox monks over the keys of the Church of the Nativity at Bethlehem, the Silver Star in the Grotto and rights in the Church of the Holy Sepulchre, with France backing the Latins on the basis of its capitulations of 1740 and Russia the Orthodox on the Küçük Kaynarca treaty, was the immediate cause of the Crimean War; the sultan's firman of 1852 and Russia's rejection of the compromise led to Menshikov's mission in 1853.
entries.note: Figes 2010; Anderson 1966; Firman of 8 February 1852; Lambert 1990.

categories.label: Expression
categories.subtitle: Orientalist painting, Byron and philhellenism, Aida and the guidebook

entries.label: Byron, philhellenism and the travellers
entries.hint: Byron's Childe Harold (1812) and The Giaour (1813), Chateaubriand's Itinéraire (1811), Lamartine's Voyage en Orient (1835), Flaubert's journey with Maxime du Camp in 1849–1851, Burton's pilgrimage to Mecca in 1853 and Kinglake's Eothen (1844) created a literature of travel, in which the East was the field of romance, danger and religion.
entries.note: Byron, Childe Harold; Kinglake, Eothen; Richard Burton, Personal Narrative of a Pilgrimage to Al-Madinah and Meccah (1855); Billie Melman, Women's Orients (1992).

entries.label: Orientalist painting
entries.hint: The Massacre at Chios (1824) and Women of Algiers (1834) by Delacroix, Ingres's Turkish Bath, and the paintings of Gérôme, Decamps and David Roberts, with scenes of harem, bazaar and slave market, created a European image of the East that Edward Said and others criticised in the 1970s as expressions of imperial power, while others see in it also a curiosity and respect for the cultures it depicted.
entries.note: Linda Nochlin, ‘The Imaginary Orient’, Art in America 71 (1983); Edward Said, Orientalism (1978); John Mackenzie, Orientalism: History, Theory and the Arts (1995).

entries.label: Verdi's Aida
entries.hint: Verdi's opera, commissioned by the khedive Ismail for the new Cairo Opera House, which opened in 1869 with Rigoletto, was first given on 24 December 1871 with a story outlined by the Egyptologist Auguste Mariette and was not, as often said, written for the opening of the Suez Canal; its sets and costumes made Pharaonic Egypt a theme of European popular culture.
entries.note: Julian Budden, The Operas of Verdi vol. 3 (1981); Mariette's scenario; Egyptian court records.

categories.label: Thought
categories.subtitle: The concept of the Eastern Question, Orientalism and its critics, the archaeologists and the decipherers

entries.label: The Orientalists and their critics
entries.hint: The establishment of the Société asiatique (1822), the first chairs of Arabic and Persian and the learned works of Silvestre de Sacy, Edward Lane's Manners and Customs of the Modern Egyptians (1836), Ignaz Goldziher and Snouck Hurgronje built the scholarly study of Islam; the question of whether their knowledge was in the service of empire, raised by Said in 1978, remains a main debate in the field.
entries.note: Said 1978; Robert Irwin, For Lust of Knowing (2006); Albert Hourani, Islam in European Thought (1991).

entries.label: The Eastern Question as a concept
entries.hint: The phrase la question d'Orient first appeared in the discussions of the Congress of Verona in 1822 and by the 1830s meant the problem of the future of the Ottoman Empire and its territories, a European diplomatic concept that treated its subjects as objects; historians such as Anderson and Mark Mazower note that this view downplays the empire's own reforms and the agency of its peoples.
entries.note: Anderson 1966; Alexander Lee Macfie, The Eastern Question 1774–1923 (1989); Mark Mazower, The Balkans (2000).

entries.label: The archaeologists of Nineveh and Behistun
entries.hint: Paul-Émile Botta excavated Khorsabad from 1843 and Austen Henry Layard Nimrud and Nineveh from 1845, sending Assyrian reliefs to the Louvre and the British Museum, while Henry Rawlinson copied the trilingual Behistun inscription of Darius (1835–1847) at the risk of his life and with Hincks and Oppert deciphered Akkadian cuneiform by 1851; the discoveries confirmed Biblical Nineveh and began Assyriology.
entries.note: Layard, Nineveh and Its Remains (1849); Rawlinson, ‘The Persian Cuneiform Inscription at Behistun’ (1846–1851); Mogens Trolle Larsen, The Conquest of Assyria (1996).

entries.label: The French and English archaeology of the Holy Land
entries.hint: The Palestine Exploration Fund, founded in 1865, with the survey of Western Palestine by Conder and Kitchener (1871–1877) and the Jerusalem excavations of Charles Warren, and the French Ecole Biblique (1890), set out to map and document the land of the Bible, with the Moabite Stone, the Siloam inscription (1880) and Tell el-Hesi (Petrie 1890) as its early discoveries.
entries.note: Neil Silberman, Digging for God and Country (1982); Warren, The Recovery of Jerusalem (1871); Petrie, Tell el Hesy (1891).

categories.label: Economy
categories.subtitle: The free-trade treaties, the Ottoman and Egyptian debts, the Suez shares and the Régie

entries.label: The Levant trade and the new export economies
entries.hint: Ottoman trade with Europe grew many times over in the first half of the nineteenth century, in raw materials such as cotton, silk, grain and tobacco exported and manufactures imported; the ports of Izmir, Beirut, Salonica and Alexandria grew into cosmopolitan cities with European merchant houses, and the local handicrafts, such as the textile weavers of Aleppo, declined, as Donald Quataert and Reşat Kasaba show.
entries.note: Reşat Kasaba, The Ottoman Empire and the World Economy (1988); Donald Quataert, The Ottoman Empire 1700–1922 (2000); Pamuk 1987.

entries.label: The Ottoman and Egyptian debts
entries.hint: The Ottoman state took its first foreign loan in 1854, and by 1875 had a debt of some 200 million pounds, of which much went to service older loans; Egypt's debt under Said and Ismail rose from 3 million pounds in 1863 to 90 million by 1876, and the default of both states led to the dual control of Egypt (1876) and the Ottoman Public Debt Administration (1881), which put revenues under foreign supervision.
entries.note: Pamuk 1987; David Landes, Bankers and Pashas (1958); Donald Blaisdell, European Financial Control in the Ottoman Empire (1929).

entries.label: The Suez shares and the Régie
entries.hint: In November 1875 Disraeli, using a loan from the Rothschilds, bought the khedive Ismail's 176,602 shares in the Suez Canal Company for £3,976,582, giving Britain 44 per cent; in 1883 the Ottoman tobacco monopoly, the Régie, was set up by a company of European bondholders, an example of the foreign financial control of the 1880s.
entries.note: Blake 1966; Landes 1958; Edhem Eldem, A History of the Ottoman Bank (1999).

categories.label: Technology
categories.subtitle: The steamship, the telegraph, the canal and the railways

entries.label: The steamship and the Euphrates expedition
entries.loc: The Euphrates and the Red Sea
entries.hint: Francis Chesney's expedition of 1835–1837 took two steamers, the Euphrates and the Tigris, to the Euphrates to see if a river route to India was possible, with the loss of the Tigris in a storm; steamers on the Red Sea and Gulf from 1830, the Suez overland route of Thomas Waghorn and the Peninsular and Oriental line cut the time from England to India to forty days.
entries.note: Francis Chesney, Narrative of the Euphrates Expedition (1868); Anderson 1966; Daniel Headrick, The Tools of Empire (1981).

entries.label: The telegraph to India
entries.hint: The first Ottoman telegraph line was laid in 1855 for the Crimean War, and Britain and the Ottomans built the line to Baghdad and Fao in 1861–1865; the Indo-European Telegraph via Persia, laid by Siemens in 1868–1870, reduced the time of messages between London and Calcutta to hours.
entries.note: Headrick 1981; Yakup Bektaş, ‘The Sultan's Messenger’, Technology and Culture 41 (2000); Anderson 1966.

entries.label: Railways of the Ottoman lands
entries.hint: The first Ottoman railway, Izmir–Aydın, begun in 1856 by British interests, the Alexandria–Cairo line (1856) of Robert Stephenson, and the Anatolian Railway of the Deutsche Bank from 1888 to Konya in 1896 and the 1903 concession to Baghdad made the railway a form of influence; the Ottoman network grew from a few hundred kilometres in 1860 to some 5,000 by 1914.
entries.note: Quataert 2000; Murat Özyüksel, The Berlin–Baghdad Railway (2014); Pamuk 1987.
keywords: Anatolian Railway of the Deutsche Bank

entries.label: The Suez Canal
entries.hint: Ferdinand de Lesseps obtained a concession from the viceroy Said in 1854, formed the company in 1858 and began work in 1859 with forced Egyptian labour, 20,000 at a time, until Ismail ended the corvée in 1863 and the work became mechanical; the canal opened on 17 November 1869 with the Empress Eugénie, cutting 7,000 kilometres from the voyage from Britain to India and making Egypt a global crossroads.
entries.note: Zachary Karabell, Parting the Desert (2003); Landes 1958; Caroline Piquet, Histoire du canal de Suez (2009).

categories.label: Exchange
categories.subtitle: The embassies, the consuls, the concessions and the mixed commissions

entries.label: The dragomans and the embassies
entries.hint: The embassies of the powers at Istanbul, with their dragomans, who were often Levantine or Phanariot Greeks, Armenians and Jews, the consulates of each port and the system of protégés (berat holders), whose numbers in some Ottoman ports reached tens of thousands, gave the powers an influence which the Ottoman government tried to limit; the sultan's own ambassadors and the Ottoman foreign ministry were by the 1850s of European type.
entries.note: Anderson 1966; Davison 1963; Philip Mansel, Constantinople (1995).

entries.label: The mixed commissions and the Lebanese settlement
entries.hint: After the civil strife of Mount Lebanon in 1840–1845 and 1860 the powers arranged a double qaimaqamate in 1843 and then, by the Règlement organique of 1861, a Mount Lebanon mutasarrifate under a Christian Ottoman governor responsible to the Porte with the guarantee of the five powers, which had a council of the confessions, a model of the later Lebanese system.
entries.note: Leila Fawaz, An Occasion for War (1994); Règlement organique (1861); Ussama Makdisi, The Culture of Sectarianism (2000).

entries.label: The concessions
entries.hint: The grant of a concession for the Reuter monopoly of Persian railways, mines and banks in 1872, which a revolt in Tehran forced the shah to cancel in 1873, the Persian tobacco concession to Major Talbot of 1890, which led to the Tobacco Protest of 1891–1892, and the Ottoman concessions for ports, railways and mines show the pattern of foreign economic penetration.
entries.note: Nikki Keddie, Religion and Rebellion in Iran: The Tobacco Protest (1966); Anderson 1966; Pamuk 1987.

categories.label: World
categories.subtitle: The cholera pandemics, the muhacir and the Algerian conquest

entries.label: The Algerian and Tunisian loss and the Maghreb
entries.hint: The French conquest of Algeria began a long war in which perhaps a fifth to a third of the population is estimated to have died by 1872 of war, famine and disease, with European settlers' land seizure; French power spread to Tunisia in 1881 and the British occupation of Egypt in 1882 completed the loss of the Ottoman provinces on the African coast, apart from Libya.
entries.note: Kamel Kateb, Européens, indigènes et juifs en Algérie (2001); Benjamin Stora, Histoire de l'Algérie coloniale (1991); Anderson 1966.

entries.label: The cholera pandemics and the quarantines
entries.hint: Cholera reached the Near East in 1831 from India with the pilgrim traffic and killed many thousands in Mecca (1831, 1846, 1865, 1883), Egypt (1831, 1848, 1865) and Istanbul, and the Hajj was the road of its spread; the International Sanitary Conferences of 1851–1903 and the Ottoman quarantines, with the European doctors on its councils, led to the new system of public health, with powers contesting its control.
entries.note: Valeska Huber, ‘The Unification of the Globe by Disease?’, Historical Journal 49 (2006); Michael Dols; Nükhet Varlık.

entries.label: The muhacir and the expulsions
entries.loc: The Black Sea and the Balkans
entries.hint: The wars of the powers and the nationalist movements drove some 5 million Muslims from the Crimea, the Caucasus, the Balkans and the Russian Black Sea coast into the empire between 1856 and 1914, with peaks in 1864 and 1877–1878, a human toll of hundreds of thousands in the voyage and the camps, and their resettlement in Anatolia and Syria transformed its social composition and politics.
entries.note: Kemal Karpat, Ottoman Population 1830–1914 (1985); Justin McCarthy, Death and Exile (1995); Isa Blumi, Reinstating the Ottomans (2011).

categories.label: Lives
categories.subtitle: Nightingale at Scutari, Lady Hester Stanhope, the dragomans and the travellers

entries.label: The dragomans and the Levantine families
entries.hint: The Levantines, the Catholic descendants of Genoese and Venetian merchants in Galata, Izmir and Aleppo, together with Greek, Armenian and Jewish families such as the Camondos, Zographos and Baltazzis, served as dragomans, merchants and bankers between the powers and the Porte, with their own schools, clubs and churches; the Levantine world of the nineteenth century was the setting of the cosmopolitan cities.
entries.note: Mansel 1995; Eldem 1999; Philip Mansel, Levant (2010).

entries.label: Lady Hester Stanhope and the women travellers
entries.hint: Lady Hester Stanhope, niece of William Pitt, who left Britain in 1810 and settled in a convent at Joun in the Lebanon in 1818, dressed as a Bedouin, entered Palmyra in 1813 and held a court of local chiefs until her death in 1839 in debt; she and later travellers, such as Lady Anne Blunt and Isabel Burton, are among the Western women who travelled and wrote on the East.
entries.note: Kirsten Ellis, Star of the Morning (2008); Melman 1992; Meryl Gordon, Lady Hester Stanhope (2005).

entries.label: The Jews of the Damascus Affair
entries.hint: In February 1840 the disappearance of a Capuchin friar, Father Thomas, and his servant in Damascus led the French consul Ratti-Menton and the governor Sharif Pasha to accuse the city's Jews of ritual murder, arrest and torture several, of whom two died, and the case, in which the European press and governments took sides, was ended by the intervention of Montefiore and Crémieux and a firman of the sultan in November 1840.
entries.note: Frankel 1997; Tuchman 1956; Montefiore's diaries; Firman of 6 November 1840.

entries.label: Florence Nightingale at Scutari
entries.hint: Florence Nightingale and 38 nurses came to the British base hospital at Scutari in November 1854, where they found the Barrack Hospital with filth and lack of supplies, and by statistics and reforms cut the mortality, which had been over 40 per cent in the first months; the Crimean War was the occasion of the modern nursing profession and of the first systematic data on military hospital deaths.
entries.note: Nightingale, Notes on Matters Affecting the Health of the British Army (1858); Mark Bostridge, Florence Nightingale (2008).
